Yom Kippur. The Day of Atonement is the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, falling on the tenth day of Tishrei in September or October. It concludes the High Holy Days period begun at Rosh Hashanah. Jews observe it through fasting, prayer, and repentance, seeking forgiveness for sins against God and reconciliation with others.

Complete fasting, with no food or drink, lasts twenty-five hours from sunset to nightfall and is observed even by secular Jews. Five daily prayer services are held, more than any other Jewish holiday, emphasizing the day's spiritual intensity. The Kol Nidrei prayer, chanted at the start of the evening service, is perhaps the most recognizable Jewish liturgy outside of formal worship. White garments are traditionally worn, symbolizing purity and a break from everyday life.

Reconciliation with others is considered essential; forgiveness from humans cannot be granted by God alone. The holiday originates in biblical law requiring a day of atonement for the nation, performed by the High Priest in the ancient Temple. Yizkor, memorial prayers for the dead, are recited, making it also a day to remember those who have passed. The shofar is sounded at the end of the holiday, marking both the conclusion and the beginning of a spiritually renewed year. This central observance to Jewish spiritual practice and theology begins the period of judgment and repentance originally centered on the High Priest's service in the Temple, with its biblical basis found in Leviticus.
